body:
“It: Welcome to Derry” has been renewed for Season 2 at HBO.

	The show originally premiered on HBO Max on Oct. 26, 2025. It is based on Stephen King’s “It” novel and builds on the two-part “It” film reboot from 2017 and 2019. The show serves as a prequel to the films.

	The first season is mostly set in 1962 in the fictional town of Derry, Maine, and details earlier experiences the town’s residents had with the evil shape-shifting clown, Pennywise. Season 2 goes back in time to 1935 and takes place during the Great Depression. Per the logline, the story “centers on the bloody massacre of the Bradley Gang, a group of bank robbers who stop in Derry to buy ammo and end up facing unimaginable horror.” The Bradley Gang Massacre is one of the interludes in King’s original novel.
	

	The series was developed for television by filmmakers Andy Muschietti, Barbara Muschietti and Jason Fuchs, all of whom worked on the new “It” films. Brad Caleb Kane, who served as co-showrunner of Season 1 with Fuchs, is the sole showrunner of Season 2.


	Casting has not yet been announced for Season 2, but the cast for Season 1 included Jovan Adepo, Taylour Paige, Chris Chalk, James Remar, Stephen Rider, Madeleine Stowe and Rudy Mancuso, with Bill Skarsgård reprising his role as Pennywise.

	Andy Muschietti directed multiple episodes of the first season. He and Barbara Muschietti executive produce through their Double Dream production company along with Kane, Roy Lee, Dan Lin, Jamie Travis and Dhana Gilbert. It is produced by HBO and Warner Bros. Television.

	Andy Muschietti told Variety earlier this month that a writers’ room had opened for Season 2, even though a renewal had not yet been formally announced. “There’s gonna be a lot of that depression-era hustling in the air in our characters. Everybody’s trying to get by and survive the circumstances. They are gonna do crazy things,” Muschietti said. “And of course, the social, cultural, horrible things that were happening in the era, too. We’re not going to skip those. [They are the] very center and the heart of our story.”
	

	While Season 1 focused on the evil lurking underneath suburban comfort, Season 2 will have a different aesthetic. “In this case, on the surface, Derry is a graveyard almost. It’s a carcass of something because people are depleted, poor, tired, jobless, homeless. The kids don’t have a suburban, comforting life,” Muschietti said. “They’re in a very different situation. Some of them are orphans or runaways, and so the environment is pretty bleak. But there’s always the aspect of hope that is always there, burning, and it’s what keeps our new group going.”

	The co-creator had previously told Variety of his three-season plan for “Welcome to Derry,” which would include an additional chapter on the book’s 1908-set interlude.

title: Disneyland Paris to Welcome ‘The Lion King’ Animatronics, Re-Themed Space Mountain and New Parade

body:
Disneyland Paris may have just launched a new World of Frozen land earlier this year but it’s already looking towards its next land, which is set to be inspired by “The Lion King.”

	Imagineers offered fans a sneak peek of the attraction at the D23 expo in Anaheim over the weekend, including a look at concept art featuring an animatronic Scar.



	

					Concept art of the upcoming Disneyland Paris expansion themed after ‘The Lion King’ (Courtesy of The Walt Disney Company)
	



	The ride will bring to life the iconic scene in the 1994 animated classic, where Scar confronts his royal nephew. Set in a new 30,000 square metre area designed to reflect an African savanna, it will include attractions, stores, restaurants and character interactions.
	

	Although no opening date was announced for the highly-anticipated area, which will be the first in Disney’s global stable of immersive properties to be entirely dedicated to the big cat movie, construction is well under way at Disney Adventure World, one of two parks at the Disney’s French outpost.


	“The teams at Walt Disney Imagineering, Disneyland Paris and Disney Animation are hard at work bringing to life the beloved world of ‘The Lion King,’ which has captivated audiences for more than three decades,” said Michel den Dulk, VP portfolio executive at Walt Disney Imagineering Paris. “We believe this epic story was also embraced thanks to its unforgettable villain, so we are excited to lift the curtain on Scar’s presence in this major attraction. Thanks to an extraordinary level of detail, our guests will experience the very heart of the film’s story, its emotion and thrills, in an entirely new way.”
	



	

					Concept art of the new parade at Disneyland Paris (courtesy of The Walt Disney Company)
	



	In the meantime, visitors to the Paris-adjacent resort will have other attractions to look forward to. An “Up”-inspired ride called Wilderness Explorers Sky Swings will open next year while in 2028 Space Mountain is set to be re-themed, returning to its original 1995 version “De la Terre à la Lune” (“From the Earth to the Moon”) based on Jules Verne’s novel of the same name. (For the past ten years it has been themed to “Star Wars” as “Hyperspace Mountain.”) The ride will close towards the end of next year to accommodate the update, which will see a new spin on the original steampunk theme. Steve Bramson’s original score is also set to be fully remastered as part of the refurb.

	Also in 2028, for the first time since 2017 Disneyland Paris will debut a unique new daytime parade led by Mickey Mouse and friends. It will include eight new floats with beloved characters from films including “Aladdin,” “The Princess and the Frog,” “Rapunzel” and “Coco.” By the time of its launch, it will have required more than 10,000 hours of research and technical development and 225 sketches of costumes, wigs and makeup.

	“A new dawn of storytelling is upon us at Disneyland Paris,” said Christophe Murphy, president of Disneyland Paris. “From a vibrant daytime parade and a classic comeback for Space Mountain in Disneyland Park to the continued development of a themed area inspired by ‘The Lion King’ in Disney Adventure World, we are investing in the stories our guests love while continuing to evolve what a Disney visit can be. By listening to our fans and never standing still, I’m confident we are creating experiences that will delight people for years to come.”

title: Webtoon Entertainment Dives into Vertical Shorts, Setting ‘Love Bites’ and ‘Maybe Meant to Be’ as Microdramas

body:
Webtoon Entertainment is embracing the vertical media boom with its initiative to craft microdramas out of some of its most popular properties including romantic dramas “Love Bites” and “Maybe Meant to Be.”

	The move demonstrates the fast-growing appeal of short-form vertical video, even for a company that is also on the cutting edge of the scrolling graphic novel format.

	Webtoon has dubbed the genre “Short Dramas” that will run 40 to 50 episodes, with each installment running one to two minutes. A handful of episodes will be available for free before a pay-per-episode format kicks in with coin tokens required to “unlock” future episodes. The titles are available as of today and are available in English and French.
	

	Here are descriptions of Webtoon’s initial Short Drama slate, as described by Webtoon:



	“Love Bites”: When a shy 17-year-old vampire falls for the charming new boy in class, he discovers his crush is a werewolf – his species’ sworn enemy – forcing him to choose between love and loyalty. Based on the “Love Bites” webcomic adaptation of the romance Wattpad webnovel “Bite Me,” which has reached over 146 million global views.

	“Maybe Meant to Be:” After years of pressure to settle down, a struggling freelancer impulsively proposes a marriage of convenience to her childhood friend – only to discover that their fake marriage may lead to true love. Based on the romance webcomic, “Maybe Meant to Be,” which has reached over 650 million global views.

	“Swolemates“: When a cocky influencer and nerdy gamer girl start training together, an unlikely friendship pushes them beyond their comfort zones – and into an unexpected romance. Based on the comedy webcomic, “Swolemates,” which has reached over 60 million global views.

	“Rules for Dating Trash“: After a toxic ex shatters her trust, a college student returns to campus determined to swear off dating – until an irresistible bad boy challenges every rule she’s made for herself. Based on the romance webcomic, “Rules for Dating Trash,” which has reached over 140 million global views.

	“Dirty Deeds“: A young maid’s quiet life at a mystical retreat for the wealthy is upended when the brash heir to a powerful conglomerate arrives, forcing her to confront a traumatic past and sparking an improbable romance that threatens to destroy them both. Based on the romance webcomic, Dirty Deeds, which has reached over 187 million global views.

	“I’ll Marry Your Brother”: After her cheating husband betrays her and steals her family’s company, a wealthy heiress wakes up five years in the past on her wedding day, vowing to take revenge by destroying him at any cost – even if it means marrying his older brother. Based on the romance webcomic, “I’ll Marry Your Brother,” which has reached over 73 million global views.


	Webtoon boasts 155 million monthly active users across an array of titles that have been adapted for traditional TV and movies. The company was founded in South Korea in 2005. Webtoon had a U.S. IPO in 2024.

	(Pictured: “Maybe Meant to Be”)

title: American Independent Film Production Is Dying. Jeff Nichols Wants to Save It.
description: Jeff Nichols is not only one of cinema’s foremost chroniclers of the American South, but is doing his damnedest to revitalize the film scene in his
body:
Jeff Nichols is not only one of cinema’s foremost chroniclers of the American South, but is doing his damnedest to revitalize the film scene in his hometown of Little Rock, Arkansas.

	When he brought his acclaimed film “Loving” — about the landmark Loving v. Virginia case that legalized interracial marriage nationwide — to Little Rock back in 2016, he surveyed the scene and didn’t like what he saw.


	“I wanted to bring it to my hometown and show them what I’d done and there was no email list or any central grouping of anyone interested in film,” recalls Nichols.
	

	So, over drinks with his former high school classmate Kathryn Tucker, they hatched a plan to start the Arkansas Cinema Society and its film festival Filmland in order to foster a film community in Arkansas. Nichols was inspired by what Richard Linklater had accomplished with the Austin Film Society and its impact on the local film scene in Austin, Texas, where Nichols resides.

	“For me, some of the biggest barriers to being a filmmaker were confidence-related and not being able to set eyes on anyone that had done it before; it puts up this invisible wall that makes it seem unattainable,” explains Nichols. But landing an internship with The American Pavilion during Cannes made being a filmmaker seem possible.

	“I started to break down those barriers and think, ‘There’s no reason why a kid from Little Rock, the son of a man who ran a furniture store, couldn’t be in the film business.’ A big part of the Cinema Society is bringing people here who make movies so people can listen to them and lay eyes on them,” he adds.
	

	The 2026 edition of Filmland, which ran Aug. 12-16, saw a number of actors and filmmakers descend upon Little Rock, including Matthew McConaughey, the star of Nichols’ riveting film “Mud,” which helped kick-start what came to be known as the McConaissance. McConaughey was on hand to screen his latest film “The Rivals of Amziah King,” participate in a career-spanning conversation with Nichols and receive Variety’s Legend & Groundbreaker Award.

	Variety sat down with Nichols — the man behind films such as “Take Shelter,” “Midnight Special” and “The Bikeriders” — to discuss the unfortunate state of independent film production in America and the rumors swirling around Margaret Qualley and Drew Starkey, the stars of his upcoming thriller “King Snake,” out next year.
	
		You shot your recent film, “King Snake,” down here in Arkansas, right?	

	“King Snake” wouldn’t have been able to be here without the work of this whole film community, and honestly, the work of the governor and different legislators to push film subsidies and make it happen.
	
		Now, shooting in America is—	

	Nearly impossible, and especially independent film. We scouted Vancouver just out of necessity.
	
		So why are we seeing so many productions move to Canada or England or Eastern Europe? Because that’s obviously hurting jobs and the film community in America.	

	It’s devastating. Studios negotiate contracts with these guilds and unions, and I suppose when they make agreements that they don’t ultimately want to pay for the results of they take production elsewhere. I’ve been in Georgia, and from what I’ve heard it’s been a pretty devastating blow with Disney taking everything to London; the work there has been challenging since this last round of strikes and everything else. The thing is, American independent filmmakers do have to abide by those contracts — and they weren’t built for us. We really need to look, as an industry, at independent film production — what it provides, what it costs — and we need more flexibility in those contracts, and more flexibility from our unions and our guilds in order to make things at different price points so that as independent film producers we have a fighting chance to keep things in the U.S. The truth is, as state-based subsidies continue to change and move, that’s not enough. We have to find ways to have independent film producers stay in the United States, and it’s a massive challenge, so that in between the big studio films there’s a thriving ecosystem of film.
	



	

					Jeff Nichols directing Matthew McConaughey on the set of “Mud.”
									©Roadside Attractions/Courtesy Everett Collection
	


	
		What are some other concrete steps that could be taken to bring independent filmmaking back to America besides rethinking those guild and union contracts?	

	A federal tax incentive would be a pretty fascinating thing to look at, which has been floated, that you could layer on top of state incentives. You’re competing against places that offer various tax incentives, but the reason why productions are going to these other places is because of the exchange rate and incentives, sure, but they’re not taking American crews and getting cheaper labor. So, at some point, that issue has to be addressed. Everybody needs to make a living and inflation is crazy, but we have to find flexibility in the budget level. You have different-tiered films and those budget levels haven’t changed in a really long time.
	
		What do you make of “Obsession,” which has made $500 million worldwide against a budget of $750,000? You also had “Backrooms,” which was made for $10 million and is now A24’s highest-grossing movie.	

	I think it’s great. I actually visited the set of “Backrooms” when I was scouting Vancouver, and the director [Kane Parsons] seemed really nice. I hope it’s a couple of things: Those films are good, and those filmmakers are good filmmakers, and they’re being rewarded for sticking to their guns and making something that spoke to the audiences they were targeting. And I don’t want to diminish any of that at all, but I really hope it’s a reflection of where society is right now in terms of watching movies. I ran into an older guy in Wimberley, Texas, in 2020, and in 2015 they’d had a massive flood there that was tragic and several people died. We were taking about that community specifically, and it seemed like in 2020, even with the start of the pandemic, that community was finally starting to bounce back. He said, “Five years — that’s how long it takes for a community to get over a tragedy.” I was really struck by the broader idea of that and here we are in 2026, five years out of [the Covid pandemic], and the world is opening back up. Look at “The End of Oak Street” and how that’s performing. Yes, you have “The Odyssey” and you “Spider-Man,” but there’s a healthy ecosystem that seems to be building for cinemas and theatrical exhibition. What’s really interesting to see is: Are these other films that aren’t horror films or blockbusters starting to show promise? And can the studios, and indie studios, start to invest in a broader spectrum of films to put into theaters? That’s what I’m hoping is happening.
	
	
		I hope so too.	

	And look: I’m from Little Rock, Arkansas, so it always seemed insane to me that movie theaters wouldn’t do well every weekend because there’s not that much to do! You know? If you’re a teenager and you want to go out with your friends, there just aren’t a lot of options other than going to the movies. I would like to think we’re reforming back into a culture that watches films. There was a period there where people were talking about how films in theaters “needed your support,” and that’s never good and not why people buy tickets. “Please come support us!” I think we’re moving away from that and it speaks to our industry as a whole.
	
		What do you think about the pending Paramount Skydance takeover of Warner Bros.? I know the DGA basically came out in support of the merger.	

	Well, I think they’re in support of reality. I think they have to be in support of reality, and the reality is, this thing is going to happen, and if you wanted to stand in the way of it, you should have done it a lot sooner. Now, all you’re doing is delaying jobs. It’s not to say, “I really support this merger because I want it to go through!” I think it’s a done deal, and of course the AG of California definitely disagrees and thinks it’s not a done deal, and I’ve read his op-ed, but… did Warner Bros. or Paramount have any of the biggest films of the last few months? It’s been Universal, Focus (through Universal), A24 and Disney. How can you argue it’s anti-competitive when the biggest blockbusters are from four different studios?
	
		And Warner Bros. lost Christopher Nolan during the pandemic by putting their whole slate on streaming as well as their handling of “Tenet.”	

	They made horrible, horrible choices with that filmmaker and didn’t treat that filmmaker with respect and got exactly what they had coming to them. I could tell you a horror story about having a big film at Fox, a sci-fi film called “Alien Nation,” and Disney absorbed it and it didn’t make it through that merger. So, I had a very personal, up-close look at it. I worked on it for four years, and it’s still something I want to make, so it’s hard to put me in the camp of, “Sure, mergers!” But I think you have to take David Ellison at his word when he says he wants to release more theatrical films through both of those studios.
	
	
		You don’t think his promise to release 30 movies a year in theaters is a bit unrealistic?	

	I don’t think it’s unrealistic at all — not with two studios. That’s 15 films per studio, and it should be 40. I think audiences are going to be there to receive all kinds of films. I don’t think it’s insane at all and it’s actually needed.
	
		I guess the issue is that there’s no way to really enforce that if he reneges on it.	

	There’s no way you’re going to legislate or negotiate that, but there needs to be some reality that comes to bear in this conversation and we need to get back to making movies. That’s where I’m at.



	

					Jeff Nichols and Matthew McConaughey at Filmland in Little Rock, Arkansas. 
									Filmland
	


	
		What was it like to make “The Bikeriders” with Tom Hardy? He plays a tough guy in that film.	

	What I found interesting was how not alpha his performance was. The A storyline of that film is a love story between the three characters, so by definition he’s in love with Austin Butler’s character. How he portrayed getting his heart broken by this young man, the same way Jodie Comer’s character gets her heart broken, I was really fascinated by. You write these roles on the page and then these actors pour themselves into them and I’m always fascinated by what they bring. And I’ll say this: There was never a take of Tom’s where you weren’t paying attention, and that is a real gift. He kind of vibrates. There’s an energy kicking off that guy that’s extraordinary.
	
		What happened to “Yankee Comandante,” your film about Che Guevara and William Alexander Morgan starring Adam Driver?	

	I love that film and I would really like to make it. It’s hard to take a movie out in March of 2020. That was a rough year! I love it so much and David Grann’s article that inspired it is so good. I’m loath to ever say movies are important, but it feels like something that’s important. Adam was going to star as William Morgan, and now that won’t happen, but we’ve got another project that we’re going to do together. It’s an important film not only about our relationship with Cuba but also our relationship with the Southern Hemisphere and whether we’re able to export our ideology. I love what the film talks about and I love that it’s a true story that’s a little bit gonzo.
	
	
		Is the project with Adam Driver the two Cormac McCarthy books you were adapting, “The Passenger” and “Stella Maris?”	

	It’s not. Those two books would become one screenplay, which I’ve written, because the books are connected. But that was with New Regency and I don’t think they’ll be moving forward with that one. It’s a challenging story and it made for a challenging screenplay. Ultimately, they were looking for a more commercial story and I think I was a little too faithful to the books.
	
		Can you tell me about your next film, “King Snake?” I’ve read it’s a psychological thriller, which sounds a bit different for you.	

	In a way, it’s a return. It’s the first original piece I’ve made since “Midnight Special,” which came out 10 years ago, so it’s really exciting in that it’s something that’s cut from whole creative cloth and completely out of my mind — and sometimes I feel a little out of my mind. I really go for it in this one, and I’m really excited to see how it plays.
	
		It sounds like Southern Gothic horror.	

	There are definitely horror elements to it, for sure, and more forward-facing horror elements than I’ve ever done. You’ve found me at a sensitive time in the process because I’m there in the editing room right now putting together my first pass, and to be brutally honest, I’m still figuring the film out. One thing I’ll say is: Margaret Qualley and Drew Starkey are phenomenal in the film. They are so good in this film and they are so good together. I guess I’m always making relationship dramas, but it’s fascinating to me how central it is to this movie. “Take Shelter” was made by a guy who’d just got married and wanted to find out what makes a good marriage, and “King Snake” is made by a guy who’s been married 18 years and we’re on the flipside of that conversation because they play a young newlywed couple and they’re still nascent, but it’s written from the perspective of someone who’s been married for a long time. There are parts of it that feel like “Loving” in terms of the intensity of the relationship.
	
		You spoke about Margaret and Drew’s chemistry in “King Snake” and they apparently got so close during the making of it that it has sparked romantic speculation.	

	I didn’t see any of that. But making a film is a really intimate thing, and you’ll understand it when you see the film, but they just really depend on each other in this film. But it’s also intimate with me. I’m sharing songs, books and films that move me, as well as personal moments from my life. To make a film like this you really have to open yourself up to the people you’re making it with. I didn’t see anything specific related to that beyond the frames of the film, but there’s definitely a lot of energy there between the two of them and I think it’s going to make the film really special.

title: Gillian Anderson Says Sony Exited ‘The Salt Path’ Distribution Deal After Authors’ ‘Fabrications’ Exposed: ‘It Felt Like Such a Betrayal’
description: Gillian Anderson has said that Sony ditched a deal to distribute “The Salt Path,” in which she starred alongside Jason Isaacs, after a scandal broke
body:
Gillian Anderson has said that Sony ditched a deal to distribute “The Salt Path,” in which she starred alongside Jason Isaacs, after a scandal broke last summer over alleged fabrications in the supposedly true story.

	Based on a memoir of the same name by Ray and Moth Winn, the book and film tell the story of a down-on-their-luck couple who walk the south coast of England after their home is repossessed and Moth is diagnosed with a terminal illness, emerging stronger and with a newfound sense of purpose.
	

	Anderson played Ray while “Harry Potter” and “White Lotus” star Isaacs played Moth. Both the book and the screen adaptation were billed as a true story.


	However last summer the U.K.’s Observer newspaper reported that key elements of the Winns’ story had been misrepresented, claiming that the couple had lost their house after Ray embezzled money and casting doubts on Moth’s diagnosis of corticobasal degeneration which sees sufferers given an average of eight years to live. The couples’ names were also revealed to be pseudonymous.

	The Winns, who won numerous awards for the book, disputed the allegations at the time.

	“It was really disappointing, a huge letdown,” Anderson has now said of the scandal. “The story came out the week we were signing U.S. distribution and Sony withdrew. We had been so surprised by its success: ‘What, really, this film about two old people going on a walk?’ It felt like such a betrayal because we’d spent time with [the Winns].”

	Speaking to The Times of London, Anderson said she has not heard from the couple but seemed to have some sympathy for them, telling the newspaper: “It must have been really unsettling, to be potentially, allegedly, not telling the truth on live TV.”
	

	She added: “I was interested in the due diligence — like, how has it come to this? What degree of proof was there? They had told us that they couldn’t talk about [a previous] legal case because it was ongoing. Anyway. It was unfortunate.”

	As Variety exclusively reported earlier this year, the film is set to get a North American release via Rialto Distribution International later this month. “This is a film of quiet power,” Kelly Rogers, CEO of Rialto, said at the time. “It speaks to something deeply human – love, endurance and the idea that it’s never too late to begin again. We’re thrilled to share this remarkable screen work with viewers in the United States and Canada and believe it will leave a lasting impression.”

	Variety‘s review, published before the scandal broke, praised the film, saying: “this portrait of loss, humanity and rebirth makes it worth the emotional investment.”

	A rep for Sony did not respond by press time.

body:
Amy Schumer is getting her teeth into another comedy, with the Emmy winner set to star in and produce “Best Divorce Ever.”

	The film comes from writer-director Sean Mullin (“Bob Trevino Likes It,” “Amira & Sam”), with Concourse Media launching worldwide sales in Toronto next month.

	Schumer will produce alongside Matthew Lee Miller and Natalie Metzger for Vanishing Angle, the production company behind acclaimed comedies such as “Kill Me,” “Werewolves Within,” “Greener Grass,” “Queens of the Dead” and “Thunder Road.” Concourse Media will executive produce and finance alongside its sister company, Archetype Media Finance.
	

	“Best Divorce Ever” follows Clarissa (Schumer) and Franklin, who after 20 years together decide they’re done with marriage – but not with each other. Determined to pull off the world’s most amicable divorce, they throw an ‘Untying the Knot’ party and eagerly embrace their newly single lives. But when disastrous dates, suspicious children and spectacularly misguided attempts at ‘conscious uncoupling’ throw their perfect plan into chaos, Clarissa and Franklin discover that getting divorced is the easy part. Figuring out how to stay a happy family is where things get complicated.


	“Amy is one of the few people who can take something as painful as divorce and make it brutally honest and incredibly funny”, said Matthew Shreder, CEO of Concourse Media. “Sean has written a smart, funny script with a ton of heart and gives Amy a great playground to do what she does best. It feels like exactly the kind of commercial comedy audiences are ready for, and we’re thrilled to be part of it.”
	

	“Divorce has a branding problem,” said Mullin, whose script was inspired by his owned amicable divorce. “I think we need to change the narrative that the only successful way to end a marriage is for one person to die.”

	Miller and Metzger added: “Sean has been a longtime member of the Vanishing Angle family, and we’ve had the privilege of watching his voice as a filmmaker grow from ‘Amira & Sam’ through ‘It Ain’t Over.’ He has a rare ability to find enormous humor and genuine humanity in the messiest parts of life. Amy brings that same fearless honesty to everything she does, and we couldn’t be more excited to reunite with Sean and partner with her as both a producer and performer to bring this film to life.”

	Schumer created, wrote, directed, executive produced and starred in the Peabody and Emmy Award-winning Comedy Central series “Inside Amy Schumer,” which also earned her Writers Guild, Critics Choice Television and Television Critics Association awards. She went on to write and star in the comedy “Trainwreck,” wile her other film credits include “I Feel Pretty,” “Snatched,” “The Humans,” “Unfrosted” and “If.” Most recently, Schumer starred in, co-wrote and produced Netflix’s “Kinda Pregnant,” and also created, wrote, directed, executive produced and starred in Hulu’s acclaimed comedy-drama “Life & Beth,” and released the Netflix stand-up special “Amy Schumer: Emergency Contact.”

	Meamwhile, Mullin is an award-winning writer and director whose narrative feature debut, “Amira & Sam,” starring Martin Starr and Dina Shihabi, earned top prizes at numerous festivals and was released theatrically by Drafthouse Films. His directing credits also include the documentaries “Kings of Beer,” “Brothers on Three” and “It Ain’t Over,” his portrait of baseball legend Yogi Berra, which was released theatrically by Sony Pictures Classics and earned two Critics Choice Award nominations and a Writers Guild Award nomination. He is currently writing and directing a documentary about Buzz Aldrin. As a producer, Mullin most recently produced “Bob Trevino Likes It,” which won more than 30 festival awards, including both the Jury Award and Audience Award at the 2024 SXSW Film Festival, before its theatrical release by Roadside Attractions. He is repped at UTA.
	

	Concourse Media’s slate also includes the ensemble crime thriller “The Smack,” which starts production next month and stars Casey Affleck, Sam Rockwell, Marisa Tomei, and Kathy Bates, and the Lucy Hale romantic comedy “Vision Board.” It recently closed global distribution deals on their SXSW-premiered psychological thriller “Sender” starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Britt Lower, Rhea Seehorn and David Dastmalchian and their inspirational drama “Maybe We Should” starring Heather Graham, Jeremy John Wells, Lil Rel Howery and Kevin Nealon.

Rosie O’Donnell is finally back behind the talk-show desk.

	Yes, the former host of “The Rosie O’Donnell Show” and “The View” will be serving as guest host of “Jimmy Kimmel Live” the week of Aug. 17 while Kimmel is on vacation (as part of his summer rotation). He said he’d tapped O’Donnell for the stint as “a special treat” for Donald Trump, given the president’s 20-year-long vendetta against her for mocking his bankruptcies on “The View.”
	

	O’Donnell tells Variety that the offer “came out of the blue,” since not only have they never spoken in person, but they had what she describes as an “adversarial relationship.”


	“We’ve never spoken on the phone; we’ve texted a few times. Howard Stern tried to make amends with us, so we’ve been at the same parties a few times and I would talk to his wife. But Jimmy was never a fan of mine, and it was kind of an adversarial relationship — not that I was fighting back, but I was like, ‘OK, one of the bro guys…,’” O’Donnell recalls.

	But that all changed when O’Donnell reached out to Kimmel following the death of his beloved Uncle Frank Potenza, a former NYPD officer who’d made a number of memorable comedy-sketch appearances on his nephew’s late-night show.

	“When everything happened with his uncle dying, I wrote him and he wrote back. So, when my publicist called and said, ‘Do you want to guest-host ‘Kimmel’ for a week?’ I said, ‘I haven’t ever even been a guest!’ And then I said, ‘If you’re positive that that’s an actual offer and he wants me to do it, then I most certainly will,’” says O’Donnell, adding, “I was surprised, to tell you the truth, and very thankful.”  
	

	Another reason O’Donnell took the gig, other than having the opportunity to air out Trump to an audience of millions on ABC, is to support the late-night community amid Trump’s war on TV comedy, one that’s cost Stephen Colbert his “Late Show” and nearly claimed Kimmel as well.

	“I support [Kimmel] in what he’s doing with the First Amendment, and our ability as entertainers and citizens to speak out against our government that’s enshrined in the Founding Fathers’ writings about our government, so I think he’s fantastic,” says O’Donnell. “And I wish that Stephen Colbert had the same kind of support when it happened to him, because he shouldn’t be gone either.

	As for the Colbert of it all, and Paramount Skydance owner (and Trump winer-and-diner) David Ellison’s pending takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, which includes CNN, O’Donnell didn’t hold back.

	“It would be like Fox taking over all news channels. Imagine if Fox was not one outlier and Fox was the mainstay? That’s what’s happening with Hollywood now and the Ellisons, and it’s tragic,” O’Donnell says.

	She then pointed to Ellison and Bari Weiss’ right-wing makeover of CBS News and its crown jewel, “60 Minutes,” as an example of what’s to come if Ellison’s $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery is approved.

	“Look at what’s happened to CBS News and ‘60 Minutes,’ which was the gold star of their entire network, and they blew it up,” claims O’Donnell. “This Bari Weiss person, I don’t know how she can live with herself. There are people who are sidling up to him and history will record all of their names, what they did, and who they stood next to.”

	O’Donnell continues, “If you’re in a room with 10 Nazis at a table and you’re the only one who’s not, there’s a pretty good chance you’re a Nazi.”

body:
Arnold Palmer once said that golf was “deceptively simple and endlessly complicated.”  Now the PGA Tour hopes to give fans of the links something a little less intense: a good laugh.

	“PGA Tour Alter Ego” a new unscripted sports comedy series co-produced with Peyton Manning’s Omaha Productions, launches Tuesday ahead of the organization’s BMW Championship. Some viewers may be surprised, even tickled, by what they see. The first episode will debut on the PGA Tour YouTube channel and PGATour.com, as well as Omaha Productions’ YouTube and social channels, and shows Wyndham Clark going incognito to test and trick fans and peers. One additional episode will follow, featuring Max Homa.
	

	“We think we’ve got a generation of really fun PGA Tour stars who are looking to connect and build their brand and their game to try stuff like this out,” says Andy Weitz, PGA Tour’s chief marketing officer, during a recent interview.


	Laughs are only one potential outcome from the golf organization’s push to create such content around its tournaments and events. Executives, says Weitz, have noticed a significant uptick of people playing golf since the coronavirus pandemic and see an opportunity to bring a younger generation of fans under its umbrella. “If they are a fan of comedy, if they are a Will Ferrell fan, if they are a Druski fan, if they are a YouTube golf fan, if they like simulator golf, if they like gaming, there are all kinds of different ways through our original content strategy,” he says. “We can make them more familiar with our players, more familiar with the competitive format, and translate that into overtime a larger fan base.”
	

	In recent months, PGA Tour has launched “Chasing Sunday,” a docuseries that gives fans a behind the scenes look at top events. “Tee Sheet presented by FedEx” offered previews of the FedEx Cup Playoffs. “The Life” helps fans learn more about their favorite players, off the course.

	In January of last year, PGA Tour unveiled a new 165,000 square foot production facility on its campus in Ponte Vedra Beach in Florida, as part of a bid to gain new oversight over thousands of hours of sports content that its top executives believe will only be in more demand in a future dominated by streaming video — and different kinds of media entities that are looking at sports in very different fashion in the streaming era,

	“Having firm control of your content strategy is really important because it becomes the bridge to your core product,” says Weitz. “We play Thursday through Sunday, and we want to own the whole week. We want to find ways to meet our fans earlier in the week, deepen their engagement and connection to the tour, remind them that they should be watching on the weekend.”

	Part of that effort involves programs such as “Alter Ego.” “One of the most fun things for us to do right now is to reach out to leading production houses like Omaha and say, ‘Where is the overlap? What are you working on that might fit in the world of golf?’ We’re open for business here,” says Weitz.

	Indeed, the seeds for “Alter Ego” were planted in 2025 when PGA Tour Studios teamed up with Omaha Productions to send Eli Manning undercover as a tournament volunteer to catch star golfers off guard at the FedEx St. Jude Championship.

	“Hidden stars causing chaos on the PGA Tour is a great setup for a fun show,” says Petyon Manning, in a statement.

	The new “Alter Ego” also comes with a sponsor. ShipSticks, which helps transport golf clubs and bags, is featured in different segments of the program, says Weitz, which requires golfers to figure out logistics for equipment.

Aug 17, 2026 9:00am PT	
	

	
		Final Emmy Voting Opens: 25 Records That Could Be Broken, From Jean Smart and Allison Janney’s All-Time Tie to Harrison Ford’s First Trophy at 84
	
	
			


			
			
	

									Apple TV / HBO Max / Netflix
	

		
	
				

	Final Emmy voting is now open.

	More than 20,000 Television Academy members have the final ballots in hand for the 78th Emmy Awards, with voting remaining open through Wednesday, Aug. 26, at 10 p.m. PT. When the envelopes begin opening — first during the two-night artisans ceremony, formerly known as the Creative Arts Emmys, on Sept. 5 and 6, and then during NBC’s Sept. 14 telecast from the Peacock Theater — some of the longest-standing records in Emmy history could fall.

	HBO Max enters the final stretch as the most-nominated network, led by two of the year’s biggest contenders: reigning drama champion “The Pitt” and the fifth and final season of “Hacks.” But the night could produce history well beyond the top program races. Two actresses could tie the all-time record for acting wins on the same night. A limited series could accomplish something no program has done in the category’s history. The competition could produce just the fourth three-peat ever — or the first for a show celebrating its 50th season. And perhaps the most poignant possibility sits in guest actor in a comedy series, where Rob Reiner is nominated posthumously alongside Michael J. Fox. Either outcome would rewrite the record book.

	Here’s a rundown of the records, milestones and fun facts among some of the nominees this year, category by category.


			
			
	Drama Series
			
										
					Image Credit: Apple TV				
					
				

RECORD: If “Slow Horses” or “Pluribus” wins, Apple TV claims its first drama series Emmy ever. The streamer has conquered comedy twice over — “Ted Lasso” and “The Studio” — but has never taken TV’s most prestigious prize.
MILESTONE: If “The Pitt” wins, it becomes the 11th drama ever to win the top prize for its first two seasons — and the first since “Mad Men” (2008-09). The others include: “The United States Steel Hour,” “Playhouse 90,” “The Defenders,” “Mission: Impossible,” “Upstairs, Downstairs,” “Hill Street Blues,” “Picket Fences,” “The Practice” and “The West Wing.”
FUN FACT: If “Pluribus,” “A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms” or “Task” wins, it would mark back-to-back freshman champions, following “The Pitt” last year.


		
			
			
	Comedy Series
			
										
					Image Credit: Apple TV				
					
				

MILESTONE: If “Widow’s Bay,” “Shrinking” or “Margo’s” wins, it would be the fourth statue for Apple, one less than HBO’s five. If “Hacks” wins, they would tick up, still in fourth place overall behind NBC (26), CBS (22) and ABC (11).
MILESTONE: If “Only Murders in the Building” wins, the Hulu whodunit finally lands the top prize on its fifth consecutive series nomination — it’s 0-for-4 to date despite seven Emmys elsewhere.
MILESTONE: If “Abbott Elementary” wins, Quinta Brunson’s sitcom also breaks through on its fifth straight series nomination, becoming the first broadcast comedy to win since “Modern Family” in 2014.
FUN FACT: With reigning champ “The Studio” sitting out this cycle, a new winner is guaranteed. If “The Bear” or “Hacks” wins, each claims its second series title (2023 and 2024, respectively). If “Widow’s Bay” or “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” wins, it’s the second consecutive freshman champion after “The Studio.”


		
			
			
	Limited or Anthology Series
			
										
					Image Credit: Netflix				
					
				

RECORD: If “Beef” wins, it makes history: no program has ever won the limited/anthology series Emmy twice. In roughly seven decades of the category’s various incarnations, every winner has been a one-and-done either because they needed to move to one of the recurring categories, or just never returned.
FUN FACT: Anything else wins — “All Her Fault,” “The Beast in Me,” “DTF St. Louis” or “Love Story: John F. Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette” — and it’s a first-time winner, as all four are freshman entries.


		
			
			
	Lead Actor, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: Disney				
					
				

MILESTONE: If Sterling K. Brown wins for “Paradise,” he becomes just the third man ever to win lead drama actor for two different shows, joining Robert Young (“Father Knows Best,” “Marcus Welby, M.D.”) and James Spader (“The Practice,” “Boston Legal”). It would also be his third acting Emmy for a third different program.
MILESTONE: If Noah Wyle wins, he becomes the fifth actor to win lead drama for a show’s first two seasons — after E.G. Marshall (“The Defenders”), Bill Cosby (“I Spy”), Daniel J. Travanti (“Hill Street Blues”) and Bryan Cranston (“Breaking Bad”) — and the first since Cranston in 2009. Wyle is also nominated for directing “The Pitt,” making him a threat to double.
FUN FACT: If Gary Oldman wins for “Slow Horses,” the Oscar winner lands his first Emmy at 68 after three noms.


		
			
			
	Lead Actress, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Eddy Chen/HBO				
					
				

RECORD: If Zendaya wins, she becomes the youngest performer in history — man or woman — to win three lead drama Emmys, at 30 years and two weeks. Cosby was 30 years and 10 months when he claimed his third in 1968. She’d also be the fifth woman with three or more, after Barbara Bain, Michael Learned, Tyne Daly and Edie Falco, and the first since Falco in 2003. She already owns the category’s youngest-winner mark (24, in 2020).
RECORD: If Keri Russell wins — she’s 0-for-5 in acting nominations across “The Americans” and “The Diplomat” — and longtime partner Matthew Rhys converts either of his two lead nominations, for “Widow’s Bay” or “The Beast in Me,” they become just the third real-life couple to win acting Emmys in the same year, and the first in 40 years, following two married pairs: Alfred Lunt and Lynn Fontanne (1965, both for “The Magnificent Yankee”) and William Daniels and Bonnie Bartlett (1986, both for “St. Elsewhere”). Russell and Rhys, partners for more than a decade though not legally married, would be the first couple to do it for different shows — and Rhys’ lone Emmy so far came for playing her on-screen husband in “The Americans.”
MILESTONE: If Chase Infiniti wins, the 26-year-old “The Testaments” breakout becomes the second-youngest lead drama actress champion ever, behind only Zendaya — on her first career nomination.
MILESTONE: If Rhea Seehorn wins, the “Pluribus” star claims a long-awaited first Emmy, three years after “Better Call Saul,” which is all-time most-losing series with 0-for-53.


		
			
			
	Lead Actor, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: Hulu				
					
				

RECORD: If Martin Short wins for “Only Murders in the Building” — his fifth straight nomination for Oliver Putnam — he lands his first acting Emmy in eight attempts and, at 76, becomes the oldest lead comedy actor winner ever, passing Eugene Levy (73, in 2020 for “Schitt’s Creek”). His trophy shelf isn’t bare: his Emmys to date are for writing.
MILESTONE: If Steve Carell wins for “Rooster,” he also breaks a 0-for-7 acting slump — famously including six losses as Michael Scott — for his first acting Emmy at 64. He has additional noms as a producer in other categories.
MILESTONE: If Matthew Rhys wins for “Widow’s Bay,” he becomes the first man since Carroll O’Connor in 1989 to hold lead acting Emmys in both comedy and drama and keep an eye on his limited series nomination below.


		
			
			
	Lead Actress, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: If Jean Smart wins, her eighth acting Emmy ties the all-time record for a performer, shared by Julia Louis-Dreyfus and Cloris Leachman. It would also be her fifth lead comedy actress win — tying Mary Tyler Moore and Candice Bergen for second-most, behind Louis-Dreyfus’ seven — and her third straight, the category’s first three-peat since Louis-Dreyfus’ 2012-17 run.
RECORD: If Elle Fanning wins — with sister Dakota also nominated in supporting actress (limited) — and both convert, they become the first sisters ever to win acting Emmys in the same year. As far as the record shows, no two sisters have ever both held acting Emmys, period.
RECORD: After winning this category when “Hacks” was on hiatus, if Quinta Brunson were to triumph again for “Abbott Elementary,” she becomes the first Black woman to hold multiple comedy-acting statuettes. She became the second Black woman to win the category after Isabel Sanford for “The Jeffersons.” 
MILESTONE: If Lisa Kudrow wins, it caps one of the great slow burns in Emmy history: she’s been nominated for playing Valerie Cherish in “The Comeback” in 2006, 2015 and now 2026 — the same role across three decades. It would be her first Emmy since “Friends” in 1998.


		
			
			
	Lead Actor, Limited Series or Movie
			
										
					Image Credit: COURTESY OF NETFLIX				
					
				

MILESTONE: Oscar Isaac would make history for Latinos if he wins for “Beef.” Only one Latino actor has won the lead actor (limited) award — Jharrel Jerome for the 2019 Ava DuVernay crime drama “When They See Us.” Since then, the only Latino performers recognized in the category have been Lin-Manuel Miranda (“Hamilton”) and, coincidentally, Oscar Isaac with his 2022 nomination for “Scenes From a Marriage.”
RECORD: If Matthew Rhys wins, note the rare feat that got him here: dual lead nominations in the same year, in comedy (“Widow’s Bay”) and limited (“The Beast in Me”). No performer has ever won two lead acting Emmys in a single year. If Rhys sweeps both, he does something genuinely unprecedented. He becomes the first man to complete the lead trifecta of comedy, drama and limited wins. The only performer with victories across all three fields is Barbara Stanwyck, whose “comedy” trophy came in a genre-blind 1961 category.
MILESTONE: If Jason Bateman wins for “Black Rabbit,” it’s his first acting Emmy after a 0-for-7 career — and he’s got three chances at hardware this year, doubling as a supporting nominee for “DTF St. Louis” and a directing nominee for “Black Rabbit.”
MILESTONE: If Riz Ahmed wins, his second lead limited victory ties James Woods’ category-best two.


		
			
			
	Lead Actress, Limited Series or Movie
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix				
					
				

RECORD: If Sally Field wins, she becomes — by a matter of months — the oldest winner in the category’s history, sneaking by Jessica Tandy, who was 79 when she won in 1988 for “Foxfire.” Field will turn 80 in November. It would be her first Emmy since 2007 and her third different show winning her acting hardware, after “ER” and “Brothers and Sisters.”
MILESTONE: If Claire Danes wins, she joins the three-different-shows club (“Temple Grandin,” “Homeland,” “The Beast in Me”) with her fourth acting Emmy.
FUN FACT: If Carey Mulligan or Sarah Pidgeon wins, it’s a victory on their first career nominations.


		
			
			
	Supporting Actor, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: Apple TV				
					
				

MILESTONE: If Shawn Hatosy wins, he claims a second straight Emmy for Dr. Abbot on “The Pitt” — having won guest actor last year — and joins the roughly dozen performers who’ve won two different acting categories for the same series. Those names include Allison Janney’s C.J. Cregg (“The West Wing”), Uzo Aduba’s Suzanne Warren (“Orange Is the New Black”), Jennifer Coolidge’s Tanya (“The White Lotus”) and Claire Foy’s Queen Elizabeth (“The Crown”). He’d be the third man in the modern era to do it, after Christopher Lloyd and Jon Cryer. 
MILESTONE: If Billy Crudup wins, his third supporting drama Emmy for “The Morning Show” ties Aaron Paul for the most in the category this century, one shy of Peter Dinklage’s all-time four for “Game of Thrones.”
FUN FACT: If Jack Lowden (“Slow Horses”), Tom Pelphrey (“Task”) or Carlos-Manuel Vesga (“Pluribus”) wins, it’s their first Emmy. Regarding Vesga on a first nomination, he would be the fourth Latino winner ever, and the first since Jimmy Smits for “L.A. Law” in 1990.


		
			
			
	Supporting Actress, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: Netflix				
					
				

RECORD: If Allison Janney wins, she matches Jean Smart’s math: an eighth acting Emmy, tying Louis-Dreyfus and Leachman’s all-time record. If both Janney and Smart win on Sept. 14, the record book gets two new co-holders in one night. Janney would also become a winner for four different shows (“The West Wing,” “Mom,” “Masters of Sex,” “The Diplomat”) — matching the all-time mark of four, shared by seven performers: Ed Asner, Tyne Daly, Alfre Woodard, John Lithgow, Betty White, Helen Mirren and Laura Linney. Remarkably, five different nominees this year — Janney, Michael J. Fox, Cherry Jones, Merritt Wever and Bradley Whitford — could each join that exclusive club.
MILESTONE: If Katherine LaNasa wins, she goes back-to-back for the first two seasons of “The Pitt” — only Allison Janney (“The West Wing,” 2000-01) and Blythe Danner (“Huff,” 2005-06) have ever done that in this category. It would mirror Wyle’s potential repeat and give the medical drama a shot at repeating both of its 2025 acting wins.
MILESTONE: If Julianne Nicholson wins, she claims Emmys in consecutive years for different shows in different categories (“Hacks” guest, “Paradise” supporting) — and becomes just the ninth woman with acting wins for three different programs in three different categories, joining Barbara Stanwyck, Tyne Daly, Allison Janney, Alfre Woodard, Betty White, Cloris Leachman, Jean Smart and Merritt Wever.
FUN FACT: If one of LaNasa’s “Pitt” castmates beats her — Taylor Dearden, Fiona Dourif or Sepideh Moafi — the show would crown different winners in the same category in its first two seasons, exactly what “The Bear’s” women did in comedy (Ayo Edebiri in 2023, Liza Colón-Zayas in 2024, but notably Edebiri moved to lead in 2024). In this category, it’s happened twice, via “thirtysomething” (1988-89) and “The Practice” (1998-99).


		
			
			
	Supporting Actor, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: Apple TV				
					
				

RECORD: If Harrison Ford wins, the 84-year-old collects the first Emmy of his career — months after receiving SAG-AFTRA’s Life Achievement Award — and obliterates the category’s oldest-winner record, held by Henry Winkler (72, in 2018), by a dozen years. If Stephen Root wins instead, the 74-year-old character-actor institution also breaks Winkler’s mark, with a career first win.
FUN FACT: If Tyler James Williams wins, the “Abbott Elementary” star converts on his fourth nomination. Williams would be the second Black man to win this category since Robert Guillaume for “Soap” in 1979, and would be the first broadcast win in this category since Alec Baldwin for “Saturday Night Live” in 2017.


		
			
			
	Supporting Actress, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Apple TV				
					
				

MILESTONE: If Janelle James (“Abbott Elementary”) or Jessica Williams (“Shrinking”) wins, she becomes the fourth Black woman to win the category, after Jackée Harry (1987), Sheryl Lee Ralph (2022) and Ayo Edebiri (2023) — three of the four coming within five years. A James win would give “Abbott” its second winner here after Ralph.
MILESTONE: If Michelle Pfeiffer wins for “Margo’s Got Money Troubles,” the three-time Oscar nominee claims the first Emmy of her career at 68, on her second Emmy nom.
FUN FACT: If Hannah Einbinder wins, she goes back-to-back for “Hacks.” She would be the 12th two-timer, seven of which were consecutive including Julie Bowen, Allison Janney, Kate McKinnon and Betty White. 


		
			
			
	Supporting Actor, Limited or Anthology Series
			
										
					Image Credit: Netflix				
					
				

RECORD: If Charles Melton wins for “Beef,” the Korean American actor becomes the first Asian performer ever to win the category — a door “Beef” itself has been knocking on, having sent three Korean American actors into this race across its two seasons, after Young Mazino and Joseph Lee were both nominated for Season 1. Melton, also a nominated producer on the limited series ballot, would be a winner there.
MILESTONE: If Richard Gadd wins for “Half Man,” the “Baby Reindeer” creator joins Laurence Olivier, Hume Cronyn and Beau Bridges as the only men to win both the lead and supporting acting Emmys on the limited side — two years after sweeping series, lead actor and writing in a single night. Richard Jenkins, the 2015 lead limited winner for “Olive Kitteridge,” would enter the same club with a win for “DTF St. Louis.”
MILESTONE: If Nick Offerman wins — he’s double-nominated this year, here for “Death By Lightning” and in supporting comedy for “Margo’s Got Money Troubles” — either trophy is his second acting Emmy after his “The Last of Us” guest win. And if he converts both, he becomes the first performer since Allison Janney in 2014 to win two acting Emmys in a single year, and the first man to do it since Christopher Lloyd in 1992.


		
			
			
	Supporting Actress, Limited or Anthology
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Sarah Enticknap/PEACOCK				
					
				

RECORD: If Youn Yuh-jung wins for “Beef,” the “Minari” Oscar winner becomes the first Korean — and first East Asian — performer to win the category; Shohreh Aghdashloo, the Iranian-born 2009 winner for “House of Saddam,” is its only Asian winner to date. 
RECORD: If Dakota Fanning wins for “All Her Fault” — her second nom in the category in three years, after “Ripley” — this is where her half of the sisters record gets decided. If Elle also converts in lead comedy actress on Sept. 14, they become the first sisters ever to win acting Emmys in the same year.
MILESTONE: If Laurie Metcalf wins for “Monster: The Ed Gein Story,” it’s her fifth acting Emmy, in a third different category for a third different show — the same three-show, three-category group Julianne Nicholson is chasing in supporting drama. And Metcalf, like Offerman, is double-nominated: if she also takes guest comedy for “Hacks,” she’d be the first performer since Allison Janney in 2014 to win two acting Emmys in one year.
FUN FACT: If Linda Cardellini wins for “DTF St. Louis,” it’s a first Emmy on her fourth career nom, spanning “Mad Men” and “Dead to Me.” 


		
			
			
	Guest Actor, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: If Jonathan Pryce wins, the 79-year-old lands his first Emmy ever and becomes the category’s oldest winner by nearly a decade, over Gerald McRaney’s 70.
RECORD: If Bradley Whitford wins, he becomes a winner for four different shows (“The West Wing,” “Transparent,” “The Handmaid’s Tale,” “The Diplomat”), matching the all-time mark.
MILESTONE: If Colman Domingo wins, his second guest drama victory for “Euphoria” ties Patrick McGoohan’s category record of two.
FUN FACT: If Jeff Kober wins, the Daytime Emmy winner (“General Hospital,” 2022) pulls off the rare Daytime-Primetime acting double — joining Cloris Leachman, whose nine combined acting Emmys include one from daytime, among the few performers honored by both Academy orgs. He’s 72 and on his first Primetime nomination; castmate Ernest Harden Jr., 73, is also a first-time nominee.


		
			
			
	Guest Actress, Drama
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: If Merritt Wever wins, she becomes a winner for four different shows (“Nurse Jackie,” “Godless,” “Severance,” “The Gilded Age”) — matching the all-time mark — and goes back-to-back in the category. She won last year for “Severance.”
FUN FACT: If any of “The Pitt’s” three nominees wins — Brittany Allen, Tal Anderson or Tina Ivlev — it’s their first career noms converted. Anderson would be, to the best of our knowledge, the first autistic performer to win the statuette in this category.


		
			
			
	Guest Actor, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: FX				
					
				

RECORD: If Rob Reiner wins for “The Bear,” it’s a posthumous victory nine months after his death in December — the first posthumous on-camera acting win since Raul Julia in 1995, and it would come 52 years after his first Emmy and 48 years after his most recent nomination, the longest gap between acting nominations in Emmy history. He broke Lloyd Bridges’ 41-year record the moment nominations were announced. One fact that comes with it is that he is breaking his father, Carl Reiner’s record, who won this exact category in 1995.
RECORD: If Michael J. Fox wins, the 65-year-old — returning to acting after his Parkinson’s-related retirement — collects his sixth acting Emmy, his first in 40 years, and becomes a winner for four different shows (“Family Ties,” “Spin City,” “Rescue Me,” “Shrinking”), matching the all-time mark.
RECORD: If Connor Storrie wins, the 26-year-old “SNL” breakout becomes the youngest winner in the category’s history, breaking Justin Timberlake’s record of 28.


		
			
			
	Guest Actress, Comedy
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: “Hacks” already made history here: five of the seven slots (Leslie Bibb, Cherry Jones, Laurie Metcalf, Kaitlin Olson, Lauren Weedman) — the most nominations any show has earned in this category in a single year, beating the record of four set by, yes, “Hacks” in 2022.
RECORD: If Cherry Jones wins, she becomes a winner for four different shows (“24,” “The Handmaid’s Tale,” “Succession,” “Hacks”), matching the all-time mark.
FUN FACT: If Laurie Metcalf wins, it’s her fifth acting Emmy and second in this category. If Jamie Lee Curtis wins, it’s her second guest trophy for “The Bear.”


		
			
			
	Directing
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: If Salli Richardson-Whitfield wins directing drama (she has two of the six slots, for “The Gilded Age” and “Task”) — she becomes the first Black woman ever to win the drama directing Emmy. The same is true if Hanelle M. Culpepper wins for “Paradise.” Remarkably, three of the six nominations belong to Black women. Only four women have ever won the category: Karen Arthur (1985), Mimi Leder (1995), Reed Morano (2017) and Jessica Hobbs (2021).
RECORD: If Hiro Murai wins the directing Emmy for the “Widow’s Bay” first episode, he would be the first Asian ever to win in the comedy directing category. He was previously nominated in this category for “Mr. and Mrs. Smith” and “Atlanta.”
MILESTONE: If Vince Gilligan wins for “Pluribus,” it’s the first individual directing or writing Emmy of his career after six previous nominations stretching back to “The X-Files” in 1997. His “Breaking Bad” Emmys all came as a producer.
MILESTONE: If Noah Wyle wins for “The Pitt,” TV’s favorite ER doctor adds a directing Emmy to last year’s acting win — becoming just the sixth person with both acting and directing Emmys, after Alan Alda, Betty Thomas, Charles S. Dutton, Donald Glover and Seth Rogen, and only the fourth to hold both for the same series (Alda for “MASH,” Glover for “Atlanta,” Rogen for “The Studio”).
MILESTONE: If Christopher Storer wins for “The Bear,” his third comedy directing victory for “The Bear” ties Todd Holland’s record for the most by any director in the category.
MILESTONE: If Lucia Aniello wins directing comedy, it’s her second directing Emmy for “Hacks” — making her just the second woman to win the category twice, after Gail Mancuso (“Modern Family,” 2013-14). Joey Soloway, who is nonbinary, also won it back-to-back for “Transparent.”
MILESTONE: If Jason Bateman wins for “Black Rabbit,” he becomes a two-time directing winner for two different shows, after “Ozark” in 2019 — while still hunting his first acting trophy. Only four directors have ever won across two scripted genres: Jeff Bleckner, Thomas Schlamme, David Nutter and Ryan Murphy. Bateman would be the fifth.
RECORD: If Mariska Hargitay wins for the documentary “My Mom Jayne,” this year’s Emmy host becomes the first acting-Emmy winner ever to win an Emmy for directing a documentary — a two-decade bridge from her 2006 “SVU” trophy to the other side of the camera. Either this category or the documentary special would make her the first person in Emmy history to pair an acting win with a documentary win.
FUN FACT: If Lawrence Kasdan wins for “Marty, Life Is Short,” the screenwriter behind “Raiders of the Lost Ark” and “The Empire Strikes Back” collects his first Emmy at 77.
RECORD: If “Saturday Night Live” wins (Liz Patrick), its 14th victory extends the most lopsided record in this story: no program has won any directing category more.
FUN FACT: If “The Late Show” wins (Yvonne De Mare), it goes back-to-back after Jim Hoskinson’s 2025 trophy — the first Emmy the Colbert era ever won.
FUN FACT: All five nominated variety specials directors are first-timers.


		
			
			
	Writing
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of HBO				
					
				

MILESTONE: If Vince Gilligan wins for “Pluribus,” it’s the same story as his directing bid.
MILESTONE: If “The Pitt” wins — it holds two of the six slots — the reigning drama champ adds the writing trophy that eluded it last year, when “Andor’s” Dan Gilroy took it.
FUN FACT: If Will Smith wins for “Slow Horses,” it’s his second writing drama Emmy for the spy series.
RECORD: If Quinta Brunson wins, it’s her second writing Emmy for “Abbott Elementary,” four years after her first — making her the first Black woman to win the category twice. Lena Waithe (2017) is the only other Black woman to win it, and Brunson’s four noms are already the most ever for a Black woman in the race.
MILESTONE: If Lisa Kudrow and Michael Patrick King win, Kudrow could take writing and acting trophies for “The Comeback” 21 years after its premiere — as good a redemption arc as the Emmys have ever offered. A win in each would make her the ninth performer with acting and writing Emmys for the same series, a lineage running from Alan Alda (“MASH”) through Tina Fey (“30 Rock”), Phoebe Waller-Bridge (“Fleabag”), Quinta Brunson (“Abbott Elementary”) and, last year, Seth Rogen (“The Studio”).
RECORD: If Lee Sung Jin wins, his second writing victory for “Beef” ties William Hanley’s category record — and completes a potential first-ever anthology repeat across series, directing and writing. Lee already owns three Emmys, all won in a single night for “Beef’s” first season; a full repeat would push him to six, extending his standing among the most decorated Asian creators in Emmy history, where multiple wins remain scarce (Steven Yeun, Ali Wong, Aziz Ansari and composer Ramin Djawadi each have two).
RECORD: If Geoffrey C. Ward wins for “The American Revolution,” the 85-year-old Ken Burns collaborator extends his own category record to five wins.
RECORD: If “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” wins, its 11th consecutive victory extends both of its own records — most wins and longest active streak in the category. It has never lost since entering the race.
MILESTONE: If “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” wins, the ABC mainstay claims this category for the first time in more than two decades on the air.
FUN FACT: If “The Muppet Show” wins, the revival special delivers the franchise’s first Emmy in 45 years — since 1981, when the original won for, fittingly, writing. 


		
			
			
	Reality and Competition Programs
			
										
					Image Credit: Robert Voets/CBS				
					
				

RECORD: If “Survivor” wins competition program, the show that built the genre finally claims the category for the first time ever, in its milestone 50th-season year — it’s 0-for-7 all time, having watched “The Amazing Race” feast during its prime.
MILESTONE: If “Dancing With the Stars” wins, the ballroom warhorse breaks a 0-for-12 drought for its first competition Emmy in two decades on the air.
MILESTONE: If “The Traitors” wins, it completes a three-peat — only the fourth in the category’s history, after “The Amazing Race” (seven straight, 2003-09), “The Voice” (2015-17) and “RuPaul’s Drag Race” (2018-21).
FUN FACT: If “Top Chef” wins, it’s the Bravo staple’s first victory since 2010 — still the only year anything interrupted “The Amazing Race’s” first decade of dominance.
FUN FACT: If “Welcome to Wrexham” wins unstructured reality, its third victory ties “United Shades of America with W. Kamau Bell” for the most in the category’s history.
RECORD: If “Queer Eye” wins structured reality, its eighth victory extends its own record as the most awarded show in the category’s history — and makes it back-to-back for the Fab Five. If “Shark Tank” wins, the ABC stalwart collects its sixth. If “Antiques Roadshow,” “Love Is Blind” or “Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives” wins, it’s a first-ever victory — including Guy Fieri’s first trip to Flavortown’s trophy case.


		
			
			
	Documentary
			
										
					Image Credit: HBO Max				
					
				

RECORD: If “My Mom Jayne: A Film by Mariska Hargitay” wins documentary special, the “Law & Order: SVU” star makes history twice over. Hargitay, a credited producer and the film’s director, would become the first person ever to win both an acting Emmy and a documentary Emmy — no performer has crossed that line in the awards’ 78-year history. The closest anyone has come: Stanley Tucci, whose “Searching for Italy” wins came in the separate hosted nonfiction category. And the timing is poetic — the documentary trophies are handed out at the Creative Arts ceremonies Sept. 5 and 6, meaning Hargitay could walk onto the Peacock Theater stage Sept. 14 as this year’s Emmy host and its newest Emmy winner. She’d be the first person to host the Emmys in the same year they won since Jeff Probst in 2008, and Probst shared the stage with four co-hosts; Hargitay is flying solo.
FUN FACT: If “Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!” wins documentary special, Judd Apatow collects his third documentary Emmy as a producer-director, honoring comedy’s most decorated centenarian-in-waiting.
FUN FACT: All five nominees in the documentary or nonfiction series category — “The American Revolution,” “Mr. Scorsese,” “Rafa,” “Sean Combs: The Reckoning” and “The Yogurt Shop Murders” — are first-time nominees, guaranteeing a first-time winner. Ken Burns’ “The American Revolution” arrives as the heavyweight, while Rebecca Miller’s “Mr. Scorsese” gives the master his own awards-season close-up.


		
			
			
	Variety Series
			
										
					Image Credit: Scott Kowalchyk /CBS				
					
				

MILESTONE: The talk and scripted variety fields have been merged into a single race, and we could have multiple winners now that it’s an “area award.” If “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” wins, the farewell is complete. Canceled by CBS and signed off May 21 after 33 years, the show went 0-for-31 at the Emmys before finally winning its first two trophies last September — including outstanding talk series — in the wake of the cancellation news. A win would be a final victory lap for the Colbert era in the newly unified category.
RECORD: If “The Daily Show” wins, the franchise pushes its total in TV’s top variety races to 12 — extending the all-time record it already holds, built on the 10-year Jon Stewart dynasty (2003-12) plus its 2024 talk series win.
MILESTONE: If “Saturday Night Live” wins, it takes the flagship variety series prize for the first time since 1993 — its more recent series-level trophies came in the now-retired sketch category.
MILESTONE: If “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver” wins, it reclaims a throne it held for eight straight years in the talk race (2016-23).


		
			
			
	Animated Program
			
										
					Image Credit: Paramount				
					
				

RECORD: If “The Simpsons” wins, Springfield’s 13th victory extends the record for the most category wins by any program in Emmy history. Matt Groening’s personal total would climb to 15.
FUN FACT: If “South Park” wins, it’s a sixth trophy and first since 2013.
FUN FACT: If “Smiling Friends” wins, the Adult Swim upstart claims the category on its first nomination.


		
			
			
	Other Potentials
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

RECORD: In the narrator category, David Attenborough — who turned 100 in May — is nominated twice, against himself, for “Ocean With David Attenborough” and “A Gorilla Story.” If either wins at the Creative Arts ceremony, he becomes the oldest Emmy winner in history, surpassing Norman Lear and Dick Van Dyke, who each won at 98. It would be his fourth Emmy as a narrator.
RECORD: Fox’s “The Simpsons” — a 13th animated program win extends the all-time record for category victories by any show. It pushes Matt Groening’s personal haul to 15.
RECORD: Netflix’s “Queer Eye” — an eighth-structured reality win extends its own category record, back-to-back.
RECORD: FX’s “Welcome to Wrexham” — a third unstructured reality win ties “United Shades of America with W. Kamau Bell” for the category’s most.
MILESTONE: Dave Porter — the “Breaking Bad” and “Better Call Saul” composer has never won an Emmy; he’s double-nominated for “Pluribus” (score and main title).
MILESTONE: Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl LX halftime show — a music direction win makes it back-to-back Super Bowls in the category after Kendrick Lamar’s team last year.
FUN FACT: Comedy Central’s “South Park” — a sixth animated win would be its first since 2013.

Hayden Panettiere
                          911 Call For Possible Overdose
                          ... Listen to Dispatch Audio
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 17, 2026
                            3:45 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  August 17, 2026
                                8:41 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Hayden Panettiere was found dead by a friend inside a South Carolina home ... and Emergency Medical Service workers responded to a call about a person in "cardiac arrest" and an "unresponsive female," TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Law enforcement sources tell us ... Hayden's friend called 911 at 1:51 PM Sunday to report that the actress was unresponsive and in cardiac arrest inside the residence in Greenville, SC.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            TMZ obtained the dispatch audio of responders sending medics to her location to perform CPR on someone who overdosed, which you can hear above. Page Six was first to report.
      
    
            It's unclear if Hayden's on-again, off-again boyfriend Brian Hickerson placed the call.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We're told Greenville police officers and EMS workers quickly responded, and paramedics attempted to resuscitate Hayden using "advanced cardiac life support." Our sources say this treatment builds on CPR by adding special medicines, breathing tubes, and heart rhythm tracking.
      

            We're told paramedics also did chest compressions on Hayden, but nothing could bring her back to life, and she was pronounced dead at 2:32 PM.
      
    
            Police say there were no initial signs of foul play and the circumstances surrounding Hayden's death did not appear to be suspicious. The Greenville County coroner will perform an autopsy Monday to determine a cause and manner of death.
      
    
            Hayden began her career as a child star in TV and film, and was best known for her roles in the hit series "Heroes" and the musical drama "Nashville." She also landed major roles in other movies such as "Remember the Titans," "Raising Helen," "Ice Princess," and "Scream 4."
      
    
            Hayden was 36.
      
    
            RIP
